title: Krishna Breaks the Butter Pot
story:
In the cowherd village of Gokula, Yasoda, Krishna's mother, was churning butter. She worked the rope of the churn with both arms; the cloth was bound at her waist, a garland of jasmine kept slipping from her hair, and sweat stood on her face, the small rings at her ears swinging with every pull. The curds turned in the pot, the butter was nearly ready, and the morning promised to be long and quiet. She was glad of it.

Then Krishna came to her, hungry, and stood close, pulling at her until she lifted him onto her lap. As he nursed, she looked down at his face and smiled. It was the still, warm moment of the day.

It did not last. The milk she had set to boil — forgotten in the warmth of that moment — climbed the sides of its pot and began to spill, hissing onto the coals. Yasoda set the child down and ran to it, leaving him alone beside the churn.

Krishna did not take well to being put down. One moment he had been warm and fed and held; the next, he was on the floor. His lower lip began to tremble. He bit it with his small teeth, angry, and looked at the churn pot — the pot full of fresh butter — and broke it. The pot fell apart, and all the butter of the morning's churning lay open before him.

He took up the butter, and since no one was there to stop him, he ate only what pleased him and shared the rest. He climbed onto the upturned mortar and sat there, out of his mother's sight, holding out the butter to a monkey — one of the creatures that wandered freely through the cowherd lanes. The monkey took it from his hand and ate it with as much delight as if it had been a feast.

When Yasoda came back and saw the broken pot and the butter gone, she understood at once who had done it. She picked up a stick.

The boy saw the stick. He scrambled down and ran — as if he were afraid, though anyone watching would have seen that his fear was half a game. And his mother ran after him.

It was a curious chase. The scriptures say that even the yogis, worn out by their long austerities, cannot reach this child with their minds — yet here he was, running through his own courtyard with his mother gaining on him. Her breath came short and her sari swung as she ran, and still she could not quite catch him.

At last he let himself be caught. And when she had him, he did the one thing that undid all her anger: he rubbed his eyes with his small hands — hands black with soot and ash — and cried, leaving black smears down his cheeks, the very picture of a wronged and sorry child. Yasoda, who had come running with a stick, found it hanging loose in her hand, her anger already gone. The butter, the chase, the broken pot — none of it mattered now.
reflection: The comedy is gentle because it turns on a real child's logic: interrupted at the breast, he takes the next sweet thing and shares it, then runs and pretends to cry. Even the line that the yogis cannot reach him lands lightly — the point is not his power but that a mother's chase is the one pursuit he never really outruns.
next_story_tease: Yasoda's anger would not last, and soon she would go looking for a rope.
hero_scene: In a sunlit cowherd courtyard, a young Yasoda chases a giggling toddler Krishna past an overturned churn and a broken butter pot, a stick raised in one hand and a half-eaten lump of butter in his.

toddler Krishna running with stolen butter
a monkey eating the shared butter
